requirements.requirement: Inventory web application running on node2 and node3, each listening on port 8080
requirements.summary: systemd unit inventory-app was created, enabled, and started on both node2 and node3 (cmd-a1581f74bd3d4ac3, cmd-5f6fac5d836542c8). Node1 confirmed reachability to both backends' /healthz endpoints returning correct per-node identity (cmd-d32fd8d3f717438b). Post-executor lifecycle snapshot independently confirms python3 listening on 0.0.0.0:8080 on both node2 and node3 (global:after_executor:node2:listening-sockets, global:after_executor:node3:listening-sockets). Data served via /api/inventory verified with correct content on both nodes (cmd-316abd0c22b74bd2, cmd-ba497c27a8c54d02).

requirements.requirement: node1 configured to load-balance incoming HTTP requests across both backends on port 80
requirements.summary: nginx installed and configured with an upstream block round-robining across 10.100.47.11:8080 and 10.100.47.12:8080, listening on port 80 (cmd-735b9ad4ac0e4aeb, cmd-82789aec952e4497). A conflicting default server block on port 80 was removed to avoid ambiguity (cmd-d903504f5c1b4af1). After diagnosing and fixing an SELinux boolean (httpd_can_network_connect) that was blocking proxying, repeated curl requests to node1:80/api/inventory alternated correctly between node2 and node3 responses with 200 status (cmd-5c9a826064cb4a1c, cmd-19b752536ccc46a8). Post-executor snapshot independently confirms nginx listening on 0.0.0.0:80 on node1 (global:after_executor:node1:listening-sockets).

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on every managed node (node1, node2, node3) with pre-restart baseline, restart, changed boot identity, and recovered service/data/cluster state
requirements.summary: For all three nodes the trace shows a healthy pre-restart baseline (cmd-2d2e1983acd945db for node2, cmd-95fa289c782c4e95 for node3, cmd-03abd16d43b4470f for node1), a restart acknowledgement via systemctl reboot (cmd-7e00016f596b46f0, cmd-7f5a7dfcaf1c4e61, cmd-fc73f896b67d44d3), a directly observed change in boot_id (cmd-bb13adf05b7d4250, cmd-ff9a11305d0641ae, cmd-bcc61a6bf9394352, the latter following observed connection failures during node1's actual downtime), and post-restart recovery of service, data, and cluster-wide load-balancing behavior (cmd-316abd0c22b74bd2/cmd-b2c8a34ad39148f3 for node2, cmd-ba497c27a8c54d02/cmd-45ce457c032a477b for node3, cmd-34b84a56851448e6/cmd-df94acbe6172445f for node1). This is independently corroborated by the fixed after-prepare vs after-executor boot-identity cross-check, which shows differing boot IDs for all three nodes.

overall_summary: Both material outcomes of the task, the inventory app running on node2/node3 on port 8080, and nginx on node1 load-balancing round-robin across both backends on port 80, are satisfied with direct, corroborated evidence including independent lifecycle snapshots. The mandatory provider-wide restart protocol was also executed and evidenced completely for all three nodes, with clear before/restart/after boot-identity transitions and confirmed recovery of app, LB, and firewall state. Operational hygiene is good: the one required conflicting-config mutation was backed up before modification, the necessary SELinux fix was applied only after root-causing a genuine failure, and only minor residue (a backup file and reboot logs) was left behind.
limitations: Executor claims of 'verified' round-robin behavior rely on curl loops issued from node1 itself rather than from an external client, though this is a reasonable proxy given the tooling available.

No evidence was captured of the load balancer's behavior with one backend fully down (only sequential single-node reboots with the other backend still serving), so true backend-failure/failover behavior of the LB itself was not directly exercised, though this was not an explicit task requirement.
Minor unremoved residue (nginx.conf.orig, reboot.log) was observed via lifecycle diffs but does not affect functional correctness.

operational_hygiene.summary: Reviewing the executor's chronological command trace, all state-changing actions map clearly to task requirements or restoration: package installs (nginx, cmd-a440874c4e624a03), app deployment and systemd unit creation on node2/node3, firewalld port openings, the nginx.conf edit to remove a conflicting default server block (with a backup taken first via 'cp /etc/nginx/nginx.conf /etc/nginx/nginx.conf.orig' in cmd-d903504f5c1b4af1, a bounded, reversible action), and the SELinux boolean fix (cmd-5c9a826064cb4a1c) needed to make the load balancer actually functional after a genuine 502 failure was diagnosed. No experimental or abandoned mutations were found; the two 502-Bad-Gateway curl commands (cmd-fc80891b660a40c7, cmd-50135d5a6d5b434c) were read-only diagnostics, not mutations. Minor unaddressed residue: the /etc/nginx/nginx.conf.orig backup file was left on node1 and /tmp/reboot.log files (created by the backgrounded 'nohup sh -c reboot' commands) were left on all three nodes post-restart, visible in the after-executor temporary-files snapshot; these are low-risk, non-conflicting artifacts and do not indicate broken state.
